topic: GMKtec EVO-X3: the 128GB Strix Halo local AI box versus the DGX Spark
thesis: The EVO-X3 turns the 128GB local-AI purchase into a memory-versus-ecosystem call: Strix Halo buys Spark-class model capacity for $3,100 less and decode speed within about a fifth, while the Spark keeps CUDA and multiplies prompt processing.
explanation_path: Open on the decision the viewer is actually making: which single box swallows the biggest open models, and what each gigabyte costs. Establish unified memory as the scarce resource before either machine appears -- model size in gigabytes is the wall, and both machines stand at 128GB of it. Then show the real split: Windows on Strix Halo allocates up to 96GB of that pool as GPU memory, while the Spark exposes one roughly 120GB unified pool, so both swallow a 59.02 GiB gpt-oss-120b with room to spare. Next the speed question, which is really a bandwidth question: 256 GB/s on Strix Halo against 273 GB/s on the Spark, about 7 percent apart, which is why measured token generation lands within about a fifth (tg32 47.46 vs 56.33 tokens/s, community llama-bench). Then the honest catch that redeems the Spark's price: token generation is the bandwidth-bound half, but prompt processing is compute-bound, and there the Spark runs roughly 2x-5x faster with CUDA behind it. Land on the decision rule: chat and budget point at the EVO-X3; long-context RAG, agentic loops and CUDA prototyping point at the Spark. Close with the physical caveat -- the 128GB is soldered, so the buyer lives with the choice.

claims.claim: The GMKtec EVO-X3 is a mini-PC built on AMD's Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (Strix Halo) with 128GB of soldered LPDDR5X-8000 and Radeon 8060S graphics with 40 compute units.
claims.source_title: GMKtec EVO-X3 Mini-PC Review Looking at a 128GB AMD Local AI Box

claims.claim: GMKtec's US store lists the EVO-X3 (128GB RAM + 2TB SSD config) at a sale price of $3,799.99, regular price $4,100.00.
claims.source_title: GMKtec EVO-X3 AI Mini PC AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 - GMKtec

claims.claim: Up to 96GB of the EVO-X3's unified memory can be allocated as GPU memory for local AI workloads.
claims.source_title: GMKtec EVO-X3 AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 AI Mini PC

claims.claim: AMD's official blog states the Strix Halo platform's memory bandwidth as 256 GB/s.
claims.source_title: AMD Ryzen AI MAX+ 395 Processor: Breakthrough AI Performance in Thin and Light

claims.claim: NVIDIA's DGX Spark product page specs memory bandwidth at 273 GB/s over a 256-bit LPDDR5x interface.
claims.source_title: Personal AI Supercomputer Powered by Blackwell | NVIDIA DGX Spark

claims.claim: NVIDIA's own marketplace lists the DGX Spark (GB10, 128GB, 4TB) at $6,950.00 and shows it Out of Stock.
claims.source_title: Personal AI Supercomputers | DGX Systems for AI | NVIDIA

claims.claim: ServeTheHome measured the EVO-X3 on MLPerf Client v1.6.1 (Windows, OrtGenAI/DirectML) running the Phi-4 14B reasoning model at 24.7 tokens per second with a 1.46-second time to first token.
ServeTheHome measured the DGX Spark's out-of-the-box Ollama at over 49 tokens per second on gpt-oss 20B and 14.48 tokens per second on gpt-oss 120B.

An owner who ran identical llama-bench commands on a 128GB Strix Halo box (GMKtec EVO-X2, same Ryzen AI Max+ 395 SoC) and a DGX Spark found gpt-oss-120b MXFP4 decode within about a fifth (tg32 47.46 vs 56.33 tokens/s) but prefill about 2x faster on the Spark (pp2048 1000.93 vs 1939.32 tokens/s), and summarized prompt processing as 2-5x higher on the Spark.
claims.source_title: DGX Spark vs AMD Strix Halo - NVIDIA Developer Forums

claims.claim: ServeTheHome notes Strix Halo systems under Windows split memory roughly 32GB CPU / 96GB GPU, while the DGX Spark exposes a single roughly 120GB unified pool instead.

analogy_candidates.vehicle: Two delivery trucks on the same highway
analogy_candidates.mapping: Token generation is cruising speed, set by the highway (memory bandwidth, 256 vs 273 GB/s), so both trucks cruise within about a fifth of each other hauling the same 59GB trailer; the Spark's ~1 PFLOP engine only shortens the loading dock (prefill).
analogy_candidates.limit: A truck's bigger engine also raises top speed, while here the compute edge barely moves decode -- say "same speed limit" explicitly or the analogy misleads.

analogy_candidates.vehicle: Soldered memory is an engine with a welded hood
analogy_candidates.mapping: The 128GB pool is fixed at the factory like a sealed engine, so the RAM decision is permanent; the two M.2 bays are the only bays that open.
analogy_candidates.limit: Extended to storage, which is upgradeable, not welded.

misconceptions.myth: 128GB of unified memory means 128GB of VRAM.
misconceptions.reality: The EVO-X3 allocates up to 96GB as GPU memory, and the Spark exposes a single roughly 120GB pool (claims 3 and 10).

misconceptions.myth: The Spark's up-to-1-PFLOP-FP4 compute makes chat much faster than Strix Halo.
misconceptions.reality: Token generation is memory-bandwidth-bound (256 vs 273 GB/s, about 7 percent apart), and measured gpt-oss-120b decode sits within about a fifth; the compute pays out in prompt processing, 2-5x faster on the Spark (claims 4, 5, 9).

glossary.definition: AMD's Ryzen AI Max+ 300-series halo chip pairing Zen 5 CPU cores with a Radeon 8060S iGPU and up to 128GB of unified LPDDR5X memory.
One pool of RAM shared by CPU and GPU, so a model loads once instead of being copied into separate VRAM.
How fast weights can stream from memory each second; it caps tokens per second when the model is generating.
How many words-or-pieces the model emits each second while answering; the speed a viewer actually feels.
The phase where the model reads your whole prompt at once; it is compute-bound, which is where the Spark pulls ahead.
The phase where the model writes the answer one token at a time; it is memory-bandwidth-bound, which is why the two boxes tie.
An open mixture-of-experts model shipped in MXFP4 quantization at 59.02 GiB, small enough for both 128GB boxes.
A cabled PCIe port on the EVO-X3 for attaching an external GPU, rarer than Thunderbolt on mini-PCs.

unverified: No EVO-X3-specific gpt-oss-120b tokens-per-second measurement exists in the fetched pages; the tg32 47.46 figure is an EVO-X2 (same SoC) in an owner's forum post, and the EVO-X3's own number is STH's MLPerf Phi-4 14B on Windows.
The Strix Halo tg32 47.46 row was partially reconstructed from a truncated forum table (community tier, medium confidence).
The DGX Spark's street availability and price at non-NVIDIA retailers was not checked; only NVIDIA's marketplace listing ($6,950.00, Out of Stock) was fetched.
The Ask HN thread "Best Local LLM Box?" (id 50039529) had 2 points and 0 comments when fetched, so it contributes no quotable recommendations.
Historical DGX Spark launch prices ($3,999 or $4,999) could not be grounded in any fetched page.
What the EVO-X3 does on Linux with ROCm rather than Windows DirectML was not measured in any fetched page.
suggested_outline:
Same desk, same 128GB, $3,100 apart: the EVO-X3 at $3,799.99 and the Spark at $6,950.00 both exist to swallow models no gaming GPU can hold.
What fits and how fast: up to 96GB of GPU memory versus a roughly 120GB unified pool (both hold the 59.02 GiB gpt-oss-120b), then the bandwidth tie -- 256 versus 273 GB/s -- and the measurements showing token generation within about a fifth.
The honest catch and the rule: prefill and CUDA are what the extra dollars buy (2-5x prompt processing), so chat-on-a-budget points at the EVO-X3 and long-context or CUDA work points at the Spark -- and the memory is soldered, so choose once.
notes: Price grounding: the first research pass reported a $3,600-$3,800 band without a quote; the follow-up pass grounded the exact string ($3,799.99 sale, $4,100.00 regular, 128GB RAM + 2TB SSD) on GMKtec's US store, and the band was discarded. Bandwidth grounding: ServeTheHome's EVO-X3 review does not print a GB/s figure; the verbatim 256 GB/s comes from AMD's official blog. Conflict kept: the llama-bench cross-machine numbers (claim 9) are community-tier and the EVO-X2 shares the EVO-X3's SoC but not its chassis or cooling; STH's EVO-X3 numbers are Windows MLPerf, not llama.cpp. The two measurements are kept separate and neither is averaged into the other.
viewer_situation: You want one box on the desk that runs the biggest open models at home, you keep seeing 128GB machines, and the DGX Spark's $6,950 price tag makes you ask whether the mini-PC does the same job.
objection: One forum owner's llama-bench table and a Windows-only MLPerf run are not review-grade cross-platform evidence, and none of it tells me what the EVO-X3 does on Linux with ROCm or how it holds up as context fills.
